$about: A lava impact burst: the flash at the point of contact, the molten tongues that erupt out of the surface, the droplets they throw and the glowing patch left cooling behind. Event-driven — nothing happens until emit() is called. Tune in the lab, then paste the exported JSON back over this file.
$surface: Height of the lava plane above the effect's origin. Higher than the water splash's on purpose: a lava surface is usually a displaced mesh, and a glow patch laid exactly on it is swallowed by the crust heaving over it.
$impact: impactScale is the master size and impactIntensity the master energy: intensity decides how many tongues and droplets a burst is made of as well as scaling the flash and the glow. The flash is deliberately shorter than a tenth of a second — it exists to hand over to the splash, not to be looked at.
$splash: The molten tongues. splashWidth is the thickness of one ribbon, splashSpread is how far they lean out. splashShapeVariation at 0 gives an even starburst, which is exactly what thrown lava never is; taper slides each tongue between a broad lobe and a thin ribbon and curvature decides how early it arcs over.
$droplets: dropletCount is per impact, before impactIntensity scales it. The size draw is biased toward the minimum, so a burst is fine spatter with a few heavy blobs arcing through it. dropletSpread is how flat the trajectories are allowed to be: 0 is a column, 1 a wide fan.
$look: One heat scalar drives colour and brightness together everywhere, so a cooling element can never end up dim and yellow or bright and red. hotColor is the core, lavaColor the body, coolColor what everything fades through on the way out. The effect is readable without bloom; it only gets brighter with it.
$variation: randomness varies the whole burst between triggers — size, energy and timing — which is what stops a retriggered effect reading as a looping animation. The secondary beat is material peeling off the tongues as they come apart, so it stays small and subordinate.
